notes: Renewed permission application on LSO decision; Hughes J refused leave and limited costs to acknowledgement of service.

enrichment.short_title: Maye v Legal Services Ombudsman: permission refused on solicitor complaint review
key_facts: Mr Maye sought permission to challenge the Legal Services Ombudsman's handling of his complaints about solicitors administering his late father's estate.
The Ombudsman investigated whether the Law Society's complaints process was properly conducted, not the underlying merits of the solicitor complaints.
Mr Maye contended the Ombudsman was legally bound to reinvestigate the original complaints against the solicitors.
Moses J had already refused permission on paper and warned that the application was hopeless.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to claim judicial review after refusal by Moses J.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; Mr Maye ordered to pay costs of £1,556.87 limited to the acknowledgement of service, not the full hearing costs sought.
enrichment.ratio: The Legal Services Ombudsman's role under section 21 is to review complaints handling by professional bodies, not to retry the merits of the original complaint against solicitors; a decision not to reinvestigate those merits is not an arguable error of law.
legal_issues: Whether the Ombudsman was obliged to reinvestigate the merits of the original solicitor complaints
Whether the Ombudsman's decision involved any arguable error of law
Whether exceptional costs should be awarded for a hopeless renewed application
catchwords: Office for the Supervision of Solicitors

confidence.notes: Short oral judgment with clear refusal of permission and explicit reasoning on the Ombudsman's statutory role.

notes: Bankruptcy adjournment appeal; Hart J restored petitioning creditor's prima facie right and made a bankruptcy order.

enrichment.short_title: Harrison v Seggar: appeal against adjournment of £2,300 bankruptcy petition
key_facts: Joint trustees in Mr Seggar's bankruptcy sought £2,300 from his wife Gillian Seggar after a void preference payment from his Abbey National account on the day of his bankruptcy order.
A statutory demand and bankruptcy petition followed non-payment; the debtor accepted at the county court hearing that the sum was repayable to the estate.
District Judge Bailey adjourned the petition generally on the debtor's offer to pay £50 per month despite no credible evidence of ability to pay.
The debtor did not appear on appeal and had made only four £50 payments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Petitioning creditors' appeal to a High Court judge against a county court order adjourning a bankruptcy petition generally for instalment payment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the district judge's order set aside and a bankruptcy order made against Gillian Anne Seggar.
enrichment.ratio: A petitioning creditor has a prima facie right to a bankruptcy order where the petition debt is clearly established; adjournment for payment requires credible evidence of full payment within a reasonable time, and a general adjournment for nearly four years on £50 monthly instalments without such evidence is an improper exercise of discretion.
legal_issues: Whether the district judge properly exercised discretion to adjourn the petition for payment
Whether there was credible evidence of ability to pay within a reasonable time
Whether a general adjournment for about four years was reasonable

confidence.notes: Compact judgment applying settled bankruptcy adjournment principles with clear fresh exercise of discretion.

notes: Split-hearing sexual abuse findings appeal; Wall LJ upheld judge's Re H and R fact findings for C and S.

enrichment.short_title: Re W S & C: appeal against sexual abuse findings in split care hearing
key_facts: Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council brought care proceedings after allegations that stepfather RC sexually abused two older children, C and S.
After an eight-day split hearing Judge Kushner found the allegations proved in relation to both girls and made interim care orders.
The family background was chaotic, disclosures emerged unsatisfactorily, and criminal proceedings against RC were discontinued after a cousin's account of retraction.
Mr C appealed on the ground that the judge failed properly to apply the Re H and R cogency standard, especially as to S.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against fact findings made at the first stage of split care proceedings under the Children Act 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; reporting restrictions continued and appellants' costs subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judge conducting a split hearing directs herself correctly under Re H and R and rigorously analyses credibility and contamination issues over an eight-day hearing, appellate intervention is limited to clear error; findings of sexual abuse against C were cogent and the finding that S was indecently assaulted by digital penetration was open on the evidence despite uncertainty whether the assault was anal or vaginal.
legal_issues: Whether the judge applied the Re H and R standard of cogent evidence for serious allegations
Whether findings against S were supported by reliable evidence
Whether reliance on witness A's video interview was a material error
Whether paragraph 113 of the judgment undermined the findings as to S
linked_authorities: Re H and R (Child Sexual Abuse: Standard of Proof) [1996] 1 AC 563

confidence.notes: Long reserved first-instance judgment reviewed on appeal with detailed reasoning, though some procedural delay and complexity affect confidence slightly.

notes: CCRC reference on rape conviction; fresh complainant credibility evidence and Crown non-disclosure led to quashing.

enrichment.short_title: R v Warren: CCRC reference quashing rape conviction for non-disclosure

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Mr Warren was convicted by a 10-2 jury majority of raping his former partner N but acquitted of threats to kill and GBH with intent.
The case turned on consent; medical evidence was consistent with either consensual rough sex or rape.
The trial judge refused section 41 cross-examination about prior withdrawn allegations against other men.
CCRC investigations revealed undisclosed prior false or withdrawn complaints, including the Northampton knife incident recorded as no crime.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission treated as an appeal against conviction after leave to appeal on inconsistency had been refused.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and conviction quashed; no retrial sought; defence costs order in principle for period before legal aid.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh evidence of a complainant's prior fabricated or withdrawn allegations of assault and sexual misconduct, together with Crown non-disclosure of material affecting credibility, can render a rape conviction unsafe where credibility was central and section 41 would not have barred cross-examination on such prior statements under R v T & H.
legal_issues: Admissibility of fresh evidence under section 23 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968
Whether non-disclosure of complainant credibility material made the conviction unsafe
Whether prior false allegations fell outside section 41 restrictions
Whether the jury's mixed verdicts affected the safety of the rape conviction
linked_authorities: R v T & H [2001] EWCA Crim 1877

confidence.notes: Uncontested appeal with detailed exposition of fresh evidence and conceded non-disclosure failures.

notes: Litigant in person patent fee dispute; Neuberger LJ dismissed appeal and granted extended civil restraint order.

enrichment.short_title: Forrester Ketley v Brent: strike-out appeal and civil restraint order
key_facts: Patent agents Forrester Ketley sued Mr Brent for £4,400 unpaid fees from 1993-94 work; he counterclaimed for overpayment and negligence.
After 22 prior applications and voluminous pleadings Jacob J ordered re-amended particulars and payment of £1,250 costs by a deadline or strike-out.
Mr Brent failed to comply with either limb; Laddie J struck out defence and counterclaim.
Mr Brent did not attend the appeal, citing stress, and continued satellite litigation threatening claims against judges and the Crown.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against strike-out orders and application for an extended civil restraint order.
enrichment.outcome: Adjournment refused; appeal dismissed; extended civil restraint order made with Pumfrey J nominated for permission applications and 14 days to apply in writing to discharge it; costs summarily assessed at £18,400.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant in person has repeatedly failed to comply with clear unless orders requiring concise re-amended pleadings and payment of costs, strike-out of linked defence and counterclaim is a defensible case management decision; persistent abusive litigation warrants an extended civil restraint order.
legal_issues: Whether Jacob J was entitled to make an unless order covering both defence and counterclaim
Whether failure to pay £1,250 costs alone defeated the appeal
Whether an extended civil restraint order should be made against an absent litigant in person
Whether ill-health/stress justified adjourning the appeal

confidence.notes: Clear procedural history and explicit appellate reasoning on strike-out and restraint powers.

notes: Connex CCTV adjudication appeal; February 2002 accord held not to release South Eastern; abuse cross-appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Connex v MJ Building: construction adjudication after Phase 9 CCTV contract

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: MJ Building contracted with Connex companies to install CCTV at Phase 9 stations; Connex South Eastern later denied liability and suspended works.
MJ accepted repudiation and sought adjudication for loss of profit on removed South Eastern stations totalling about £363,000.
A February 2002 letter with South Central restructured SC works and was treated as an accord and satisfaction.
South Eastern sought declarations that no written contract existed or adjudication was barred or abusive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from preliminary declarations on adjudication rights under the 1996 Act pending adjudication.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on question 3; February 2002 agreement did not release South Eastern from loss-of-profit claims; cross-appeal on abuse of process dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Connex South Eastern and South Central were several rather than joint contractors for their respective franchise stations; the February 2002 restructuring agreement concerned only South Central works and did not release South Eastern from claims for removed stations; section 108(2) permits adjudication at any time and does not incorporate a general abuse-of-process limit.
legal_issues: Whether SE and SC were joint or several contractors under the Phase 9 contract
Whether the February 2002 accord and satisfaction released SE from loss-of-profit claims
Whether adjudication remained available after acceptance of repudiation
Whether late adjudication was an abuse of process

confidence.notes: Detailed contract history with clear answers on joint contracting and adjudication timing, though some accord-and-satisfaction analysis was expressly left open.

notes: Lead Article 8 immigration appeals; court rejected M*(Croatia) review approach and restored merits test.

enrichment.short_title: Huang v SSHD: Article 8 immigration appeals and the M*(Croatia) issue
key_facts: Three lead appeals concerned removal or refusal decisions argued to breach Article 8 private and family life.
The IAT in M*(Croatia) had held adjudicators should normally ask only whether removal was within the range of reasonable Secretary of State responses.
Mrs Huang, an elderly Chinese national, had strong family ties with her settled daughter and grandchildren but no claim under the Immigration Rules.
Mr Kashmiri and Mr Abu-Qulbain failed on the facts; Mrs Huang's case was remitted as potentially truly exceptional.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Lead Court of Appeal hearing of three Immigration Appeal Tribunal decisions on the proper Article 8 approach for adjudicators.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in Huang and remitted; appeals dismissed in Kashmiri and Abu-Qulbain; court rejected Wednesbury-style review and held adjudicators must decide whether cases are truly exceptional outside the Rules.
enrichment.ratio: On a statutory Article 8 appeal the adjudicator must decide for himself whether removal would be disproportionate, not merely review whether the Secretary of State's decision was within a range of reasonable responses; the Immigration Rules already strike the general balance, so success requires a truly exceptional case, following Razgar in the House of Lords.
legal_issues: Whether adjudicators apply a merits or review test to Article 8 proportionality
Whether Edore, Ala and Razgar in the Court of Appeal remained binding
How Immigration Rules affect the Article 8 balance
Whether each appellant's circumstances were truly exceptional
linked_authorities: Secretary of State for the Home Department v Razgar [2004] UKHL 27
R (Ala) v Secretary of State [2003] EWHC 521 (Admin)
Edore v Secretary of State [2003] EWCA Civ 716
R (Razgar) v Secretary of State [2003] EWCA Civ 840
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Daly [2001] UKHL 26

confidence.notes: Landmark collective judgment with comprehensive analysis of precedent and statutory jurisdiction.

notes: Foreign currency charging order appeal; court held dollar charging orders valid despite practice direction preference.

enrichment.short_title: Carnegie v Giessen: enforcing foreign currency judgment by charging order
key_facts: The claimant obtained a US dollar judgment for about $1.43m against defendants who failed to pay.
Interim and final charging orders were made expressing the debt in dollars, with sterling equivalents stated in supporting affidavits.
After the dollar weakened the claimant sought to restate the charge in sterling at April 2002 exchange rates, claiming a £269,000 difference.
Master Moncaster and the deputy judge refused to amend; the outstanding dollar debt was paid in January 2005 without prejudice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to restate foreign currency charging orders in sterling under the slip rule or CPR 3.10.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; charging orders expressed in foreign currency were within the Master's jurisdiction and he was entitled to refuse retrospective amendment.
enrichment.ratio: Miliangos did not lay down a mandatory universal conversion date for all enforcement methods; under the Charging Orders Act 1979 a charge may secure a foreign currency judgment debt in that currency, and departure from practice direction preference for sterling orders is a discretionary matter not requiring amendment where the creditor acquiesced in dollar orders.
legal_issues: The conversion date for enforcing a foreign currency judgment
Whether a charging order may be expressed in foreign currency
Whether making final a dollar interim order was a procedural error
Whether Ezekiel v Orakpo requires sterling conversion at the charging order stage
linked_authorities: Miliangos v George Frank (Textiles) Ltd [1976] AC 443
A and M Records Inc v Darakdjian [1975] 1 WLR 1610

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of Miliangos, practice directions and the 1979 Act with clear dismissal of the appeal.

notes: Financial Ombudsman time-bar JR renewal refused; Auld LJ rejected late accrual argument.

enrichment.short_title: Ropaigealach v Financial Ombudsman: time-barred endowment mis-selling complaint
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Ropaigealach bought a 20-year mortgage endowment from MGL in 1989-90 extending beyond their expected retirement.
They complained in 2000-02 that the policy was unsuitable; MGL rejected the complaint and the Financial Ombudsman Service found the claim out of time.
The Ombudsman refused oral hearing and document requests and confirmed no jurisdiction on limitation grounds.
Repeated permission and appeal applications failed; Mrs Ropaigealach later died and Mr Ropaigealach pursued a new accrual-of-loss argument.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal Sullivan J's refusal of permission to claim judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the Ombudsman correctly applied the service time limits and Sullivan J's costs order stood.
enrichment.ratio: Financial Ombudsman Service limitation rules identify when a complaint arises by reference to the event complained of and are not governed by common law accrual of actionable loss; where a 20-year policy's terms were known at sale, a complaint more than six years later was time-barred without exceptional circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether FOS time limits depend on accrual of actual financial loss
Whether the Ombudsman wrongly consulted MGL on taking the time-bar point
Whether refusal of an oral hearing was unlawful
Whether refusal to order disclosure of internal MGL guidance was unlawful

confidence.notes: Clear refusal on a late limitation argument though the procedural history is unusually prolonged.

notes: Rachmaninoff manuscript ownership dispute; Tugendhat J refused Sotheby's summary judgment application.

enrichment.short_title: Rachmaninoff heirs v Sotheby's: summary judgment on lost symphony manuscript
key_facts: Sotheby's planned to auction Rachmaninoff's autograph Second Symphony manuscript valued at £300,000-£500,000.
The composer's heirs claimed title because there was no record of gift or sale during his lifetime and the manuscript was found in a Swiss collector's estate with unknown provenance.
Sotheby's applied under CPR Part 24 to dismiss the claim, relying on inference of voluntary disposal before 1917 and limitation.
The heirs had obtained an without-notice injunction preventing sale; the Swiss heir was being joined as second defendant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for summary judgment against claimants seeking declaration of ownership and delivery up, heard alongside continuation of an interim injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Sotheby's summary judgment application dismissed; the claim and defence both had realistic prospects and should proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Where ownership of a valuable historical manuscript turns on unresolved provenance and potentially multi-jurisdictional facts, summary judgment is inappropriate despite gaps in the heirs' positive evidence; a realistic prospect of success exists where the vendor cannot explain lawful acquisition and further enquiry of the Swiss heir and witnesses may yield trial material.
legal_issues: Whether the claimants had a realistic prospect of proving ownership
Whether inference of gift, sale or abandonment before 1917 defeated the claim at summary stage
Whether limitation under English or foreign law barred the claim without full facts
Whether auction confidentiality and commercial impact justified disposing of the claim summarily
linked_authorities: Three Rivers District Council v Bank of England (No 3) [2003] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Interlocutory judgment with explicit reasoning on realistic prospects and why limitation could not be resolved summarily.
